cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Hi Jake. How are you getting on with the practical teaching?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: It’s harder than I expected, but I’ve got some great classes. How about you?

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Not brilliant. I’m really struggling with my Year 12 science class.

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Are they hard to control?

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Well, I don’t have discipline problems as such. It’s just that they don’t seem to think that science has anything to do with their lives. It’s depressing. They listen to what I say, and I gave them a test last week and the results weren’t too bad, but there’s no real engagement. Q21

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Right.

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: And as part of my teaching practice, I have to design an experiment for them to do. I was wondering about something on the children’s diets… you know, asking them to record what they eat and maybe linking it to their state of health.

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Mmm. Let’s think. So your methodology would involve the children recording what they eat. OK, but you’d also need to have access to the children’s medical records and I don’t think people would be happy about that; confidentiality would be an issue. If you could get the right data, the conclusions might be significant, but I suspect it’s just not going to be easy. Q22

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Right.

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Have you thought about doing an experiment using animals?

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Wouldn’t that be upsetting for the children?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Well, the animals don’t have to be harmed in any way. It could just be an experiment where they’re given a certain diet and the effects are observed.

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Would I have to get permission to use animals?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Yes, you’d have to submit an outline of the experiment and fill in a form, but it’s quite straightforward.

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: But if we found out that, say, a particular diet affects the health of animals, the same thing wouldn’t necessarily be true for people, would it? Q23

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: No that’s true, but the findings for any experiment are going to be limited. It’s inevitable.

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: I suppose so. So what animals could I use to investigate the effects of diet? Mice?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Yes. You’d need experimental mice – ones that have been specially bred for experiments. OK, so what will your experiment be investigating exactly?

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Well, something to do with nutrition. So maybe we could look at food supplements… things like extra iron and extra protein, and their impact on health.

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Mmm. That might be rather broad. Maybe just look at the effects of one supplement, like sugar, on the health of the mice?

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: In fact, maybe the focus could be on whether mice can control their own diet. Q24

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: So, what happens when they have access to more sugar, that they don’t really need?

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Exactly. Do they eat it or do they decide to leave it?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Great. Then later on, you could do a follow-up experiment adding another variable. Like, you could give some of the mice the chance to be more active, running on a wheel or something, and the others just sit around and don’t do much. Q25

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Or I could repeat the experiment but change the type of food I provided . . . or use mice with a different genetic structure. But I think your idea would be more interesting, I might think about that some more.

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: So can I talk through a possible procedure for the experiment where mice are given a sugar supplement?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Sure. I did a similar experiment in college actually.

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Great. So how many mice would I need?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: I’d say about 12. And all young ones, not a mixture of old and young. Q26

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: OK. And I’d need two groups of equal sizes, so six in each group. And how would I tell them apart? I suppose I could put some sort of tag on one group… or just mark them in some way?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: You could use food colouring, that wouldn’t hurt them. Q27

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: Perfect. Then each group would go into a separate cage, and one group, let’s call them group A, would be the control group. So they’d just have ordinary mouse food. I suppose you can buy that?

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Yes, it comes in dry pellets.

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: And the other group would have the same as the first group, but they’d also have the extra sugar.

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Would you just give them straight sugar?

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: I might be better to give them something like cereal with it. Q28

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Hmm. Then you’d need to weigh the mice, I should think once a week. And you’d need an electronic balance.

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: But we can’t hold them on the balance, or it’d affect the reading.

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Exactly. So you need something called a weighing chamber to stop the mice from running away. It sounds complicated, but actually you can just use a plastic box with holes in the top. Q29

cues.speaker: CLARE
cues.text: OK. So once we’ve measured the weight gain of each mouse we can work out the average for each group, as well as the standard deviation. And then see where we go from there. That sounds cool, I think the students will enjoy it. Q30

cues.speaker: JAKE
cues.text: Yes. One thing…
